feedback.reason: Admission controls who can consume finite capacity, while device-side dedup protects the physical effect. A quota pass is not an execution or replay guarantee.
feedback.details: Check per-device budget and command priority before admission. Keep the queue bounded, reserve capacity for urgent commands, and return a visible defer/reject outcome when capacity is unavailable. Use stable command identity at the device/effect owner so retries do not repeat actuation. Do not return success for an unpersisted command.

messages.text: A noisy device can consume the shared budget and delay urgent commands from other devices.
Late quota checks do not protect the bounded queue from overload.
Admission limits request volume but do not deduplicate repeated actuation intent.
A success response falsely acknowledges work that was not durably accepted.

options.text: Apply per-device bounded admission with reserved safety-command capacity and explicit defer/reject results.
Use one global rate limit for all devices and return the same response regardless of command priority.
Enqueue each command first, then check whether the device has exceeded its quota.
Assume that a device within quota cannot replay the same physical command more than once.
Return success to every device and drop commands that arrive after queue capacity is exhausted.

prompt: A device control API receives bursts from many devices. Each device has a quota and urgent safety commands take priority; capacity is finite and the device must know whether to retry later. What admission contract should be enforced?

feedback.reason: Fair per-partner budgets isolate receiver behavior while preserving accepted events. Retry-After and bounded backoff reduce load; durable acceptance happens before quota-governed delivery.
feedback.details: Store events durably with partner identity. Apply per-partner in-flight and attempt budgets and honor receiver Retry-After with bounded exponential backoff. Schedule fairly across partners, and report terminal/deferred states rather than dropping accepted events silently. A global queue without tenant fairness allows one receiver outage to dominate the system.

messages.text: One partner outage can starve all other deliveries and overwhelm shared capacity.
Ignoring Retry-After increases load on an already overloaded receiver.
Quota at delivery time cannot repair loss between the early acknowledgment and durable enqueue.
Accepted durable events cannot be discarded without an explicit terminal/dead-letter outcome.

options.text: Enforce each partner’s attempt budget and Retry-After independently; keep accepted events durably queued.
Use a single shared unlimited retry queue and let the busiest partner consume workers until its backlog drains.
Retry every partner at a fixed immediate interval even when its response requests a later retry.
Return accepted to the producer before the event is durable, then apply partner quotas when workers pick it up.
Silently discard a partner’s oldest events when its quota is reached.

prompt: A webhook sender serves many partners. Each partner can impose its own Retry-After and attempt limit; accepted events must survive outages, and one partner’s backlog must not consume every delivery worker. What quota/fairness contract fits?

feedback.reason: Quota and fairness govern resource access; conditional write governs document correctness. Keep both controls at their respective boundaries.
feedback.details: Cap concurrent write work per tenant/user and schedule fairly across tenants. Every mutation still carries expectedRevision and performs atomic compare-and-swap at the document owner. If admission is deferred, return an explicit result; do not weaken CAS to increase throughput. A global queue can become a noisy-neighbor bottleneck.

messages.text: Admission does not replace the revision invariant; admitted stale writes can still overwrite one another.
This systematically starves smaller tenants rather than providing tenant fairness.
Late admission cannot bound the write load and may already have caused contention or data loss.
Global serialization can let one tenant’s backlog block all others and still needs CAS for stale edits.

options.text: Use per-tenant fair admission with compare-and-swap at the document revision owner.
Apply a global quota and let admitted writes use unconditional updates to reduce transaction overhead.
Give the highest-volume tenant the largest share of all write slots to keep its throughput high.
Commit every write first and calculate tenant quota violations asynchronously.
Put every tenant behind one global serial queue with no per-tenant fairness or bounded wait.

prompt: Collaborative editing has a bursty enterprise tenant and smaller tenants. Writes must remain bounded and fair, but concurrent writes based on the same document revision must still conflict rather than overwrite. What admission policy meets both needs?

feedback.reason: Per-SKU admission bounds contention, but the authoritative stock transaction still owns the no-negative invariant. Only commit can justify confirmation.
feedback.details: Bound the queue and concurrency for a hot SKU and return explicit 429/deferred status when its admission budget is full. For an admitted attempt, conditionally decrement/claim stock at the inventory authority. A stale read or quota token cannot promise availability. Separate per-SKU budgets keep one hot item from exhausting unrelated inventory capacity.

messages.text: Quota controls request volume; it does not establish that a unit remains available.
An unbounded backlog can exhaust capacity and gives no bounded overload behavior.
Several requests can pass the same read and overbook the last unit.
A global limit needlessly couples independent resources and harms unrelated buyers.

options.text: Bound the reserve queue per SKU but decide the last unit with an atomic stock claim.
Confirm a reservation whenever the buyer passes the per-SKU rate quota.
Accept every request into an unbounded per-SKU queue and let workers process it later.
Read stock before admission and let each admitted request decrement based on that stale count.
Reject all inventory requests globally when one SKU is hot, including unrelated SKUs with capacity.

prompt: A popular SKU has one unit left and many requests arrive in a burst. The service can queue a bounded number of reserve attempts per SKU, but it must never oversell. Which admission/write policy is correct?

feedback.reason: The quota belongs to the account and must be checked before side effects. Stable identity preserves convergence while an explicit 429/deferred response communicates admission.
feedback.details: Track request budget per account, calculate it before mutation, and define whether excess work is rejected or durably deferred. Return 429 with a retry policy when not accepted. Reuse the same submission ID for retries and store completion as idempotent state. Never return success for dropped work or 429 after the update has already committed.

messages.text: A throttled or lost-response retry can count the same completion multiple times.
Success claims an update was accepted even though no durable progress state exists.
One account’s burst can consume the shared limit and block unrelated learners.
The side effect already happened; a retry after 429 can duplicate it.

options.text: Apply a per-account budget while treating repeated completion sets as the same idempotent operation.
Ask the client to retry every 429 using a new submission ID and increment progress for each attempt.
Return success while discarding requests that exceed the account budget.
Apply one global 30-per-minute limit across all learners.
Write the progress update, then return 429 if the account has exceeded quota.

prompt: A learner account may submit up to 30 progress updates per minute. The service can return 429 or defer accepted work, but a lost response must not lose a completion or count it twice. What budget contract should apply?

feedback.reason: Per-merchant budgets and fair scheduling contain bulk load; monotonic versioned publication and an observable lag signal preserve checkout correctness.
feedback.details: Limit each merchant’s bulk update rate and schedule fairly. Keep the authoritative price revision monotonic and tell callers when propagation is delayed. Checkout validates an acceptable revision/age before charge. A larger global quota or unversioned writes do not prevent one merchant’s bulk job from starving others or a retry from publishing old data.

messages.text: A bulk merchant can consume shared capacity and delay checkout freshness for everyone.
Out-of-order bulk retries can restore an obsolete price.
Checkout cannot distinguish committed visible prices from work still waiting in the queue.
A cache can serve an obsolete revision even when a newer publish has committed.

options.text: Give each merchant a publish budget while checkout reads the latest committed price revision.
Use one global update quota and let bulk updates consume it before checkout reads can validate prices.
Accept all updates without revision checks to maximize throughput.
Queue excess revisions indefinitely but report them as published without a lag/status signal.
Let checkout trust whichever cached price is most recently loaded, without checking its revision or age.

prompt: A merchant bulk-publishes thousands of price revisions, while checkout requires a recently committed price within two seconds. Bulk work may be delayed, but published revisions must be monotonic. What budget policy protects checkout freshness?

feedback.reason: Rate limiting protects the sensitive path, but its response must preserve state semantics. Never say a revocation succeeded until enforcement is in place.
feedback.details: Apply per-user or credential-scoped limits before accepting new work. If rate-limited, return a clear 429/retry policy without claiming the change happened. If the operation already committed before a response is lost, resolve the same identity/status rather than treating 429 as undo. Revocation success remains tied to authorization enforcement, not quota admission.

messages.text: The old credential remains usable after the API claims revocation succeeded.
One abusive account can consume the global budget and block unrelated users’ security actions.
Unbounded sensitive operations invite abuse and overload the security path.
A client may interpret 429 as not applied and create another operation; rate decision must precede mutation or report committed result clearly.

options.text: Apply per-user security budgets without falsely confirming a throttled revocation or reset.
Return success for a revocation that exceeded quota and apply it later when capacity is available.
Use a single global user-change quota shared across all accounts.
Skip rate checks for password reset and revocation because a 429 might frustrate users.
Perform the revocation, then return 429 because the user crossed the request limit.

prompt: Credential changes include revocations and password resets. A user-specific budget is needed to resist abuse, but a throttled revocation must never leave an old credential authorized while returning success. What rate-limit contract is safe?

feedback.reason: Weighted admission accounts for heterogeneous resource cost and protects interactive capacity. Durable acceptance ensures accepted jobs can be recovered after restart.
feedback.details: Estimate CPU/GPU cost per job, enforce per-tenant fairness and a bounded queue, and reserve workers/admission for interactive previews. Persist job identity before acknowledging acceptance. When capacity is full, defer/reject explicitly. Count-based quotas or priority labels alone do not protect a shared hardware bottleneck.

messages.text: A few heavyweight jobs can consume far more resources than their nominal request count suggests.
Autoscaling may lag or hit hardware limits; unbounded admission can exhaust the preview pool.
Priority cannot reserve capacity after heavy jobs occupy all workers.
A restart can lose accepted work before it has a recoverable job identity.

options.text: Use weighted fair worker admission by estimated cost and reserve capacity for interactive previews.
Charge every job one identical quota unit regardless of its CPU/GPU cost.
Accept all GPU-intensive jobs and rely on autoscaling to protect interactive previews.
Mark previews high priority but admit unlimited transcodes into the same workers.
Acknowledge a transcode before its job record is durable, then assign workers based on current load.

prompt: Transcoding jobs vary greatly in CPU/GPU cost, tenants share workers, and interactive preview capacity must remain available. Accepted jobs must survive restart. What admission policy fits?

feedback.reason: A request quota limits operator activity, while cohort batch size limits impact. Auditable rule revisions and compatible persistence make rollback meaningful.
feedback.details: Set per-operator limits and cap the number of accounts changed in one cohort step. Record operator, cohort, and rule revision for each decision. Advance only after observing the bounded batch and confirming persisted data remains readable under rollback. A rate limit alone does not constrain blast radius, and a flag alone cannot undo incompatible data.

messages.text: A request quota does not bound the blast radius of each admitted rollout.
A flag does not restore incompatible stored records.
The team cannot explain or reproduce which decision caused a cohort change.
Unbounded queued work and premature success hide both capacity and actual rollout state.

options.text: Limit rollout by cohort and rate while recording each policy decision under its owning service.
Rate-limit the operator but allow one admitted change to affect all 10,000 accounts at once.
Assume turning off the feature flag reverses any persisted data format change made during rollout.
Apply cohort decisions without recording the rule revision or operator identity.
Queue unlimited cohort mutations and report each as applied when only queued.

prompt: A rollout operator can target cohorts. A broad rollout may affect 10,000 accounts, and rule decisions must be auditable and reversible without incompatible data writes. What quota/control contract should limit blast radius?

feedback.reason: Fairness controls queue access; the resource’s atomic write controls slot ownership. Keep both in the design and do not confirm at admission.
feedback.details: Bound each tenant/resource queue, schedule fairly, and return defer/reject when capacity is reached. When a request reaches commit, atomically enforce no overlap at the reservation owner. Admission and slot ownership are separate stages; only the committed transaction permits confirmation.

messages.text: Scheduling order is not the authoritative conflict check; concurrent or retried commits can still overlap.
Queue admission allocates capacity to process a request, not ownership of the time slot.
The unbounded queue can grow without limit and lacks tenant fairness.
Another admitted request can reserve the slot between check and write.

options.text: Use fair bounded admission per booking resource and preserve an atomic overlap constraint.
Assume fair queue order guarantees that two overlapping bookings cannot commit.
Confirm a booking as soon as it enters its tenant’s fair queue.
Use one unbounded global queue and let the largest tenant submit most requests.
Check slot availability after quota admission, then commit later without an atomic recheck.

prompt: A booking resource has a bounded reservation queue and several tenants compete for slots. Fair admission is required, but overlapping requests must never both be confirmed. What policy is correct?

feedback.reason: Per-index quotas bound work, while durable source writes and a measurable watermark preserve correctness and freshness reporting.
feedback.details: Apply bounded update/query budgets per index. Keep source writes authoritative even when indexing is throttled, retain change records for replay, and expose the highest applied watermark plus overload/lag. Search can then report stale/not-yet-indexed instead of deleting or denying the source record. Do not claim the index is current based on queue receipt.

messages.text: Index capacity should not decide whether source-of-truth data is accepted or retained.
This hides overload and mislabels projection lag as source absence.
A hot index can starve unrelated indices despite separate workload budgets.
Queued-but-unapplied events have not advanced the searchable watermark; unbounded backlog also hides capacity risk.

options.text: Budget index writes and queries separately; expose source durability and the processed watermark.
Reject or delete authoritative source writes whenever the index update quota is reached.
Throttle index updates silently and return a permanent not-found for records beyond the applied watermark.
Use one global query/write quota across every index and let a hot index consume it.
Persist every source event in an unbounded index queue and report zero lag while it waits.

prompt: A search index has separate per-index write and query budgets. When ingestion is throttled, source writes must remain durable and the API must report index lag rather than source deletion. What quota contract fits?

feedback.reason: Urgent dispatch has a hard short deadline; batch recomputation is deferrable and expensive. Separate priority capacity and bounded cost admission protect the urgent SLO.
feedback.details: Reserve workers or CPU budget for urgent requests before batch admission. Charge batch work according to expected compute cost and bound its queue; return deferred/rejected when full. Monitor urgent latency and batch wait time. Priority tags without reserved capacity and FIFO queues without class separation cannot prevent starvation.

messages.text: A long batch backlog can place urgent work behind minutes of computation.
A label cannot recover capacity after the shared pool is saturated.
More batch admission increases contention instead of meeting the urgent deadline.
Repeated urgent retries add load to a saturated system and do not create isolation.

options.text: Keep a reserved urgent route lane and defer bounded batch work under a separate budget.
Put urgent and batch requests in one FIFO queue and process them in arrival order.
Set urgent priority metadata but allow batch work to fill all execution slots and queue indefinitely.
Raise the batch quota whenever requests are rejected, without measuring CPU cost or protecting urgent slots.
Retry every urgent route after 100 ms until one finishes, while leaving batch admission unchanged.

prompt: Route planning has expensive batch recomputation and urgent dispatch with a 100 ms SLO. Batch work may wait, but it must not occupy every worker. What fairness and quota policy should be used?

feedback.reason: Quota admission should stop excess new work before a charge, while existing ambiguous intents retain their identity and reconciliation path.
feedback.details: Check tenant budget before creating a new payment intent. When limited, return 429 with Retry-After or a deferred result. If a provider attempt is already in flight, keep the same intent and provider key, record unknown/pending, and reconcile before retrying. A throttle response must not invite the client to create a second charge.

messages.text: The existing intent may still be pending or charged; a new identity can duplicate the effect.
The charge may already have occurred before quota rejection.
The policy is tenant-specific; global capacity can starve unrelated tenants.
This amplifies overload and abandons deduplication of the original intent.

options.text: Enforce tenant attempt limits while reusing one stable intent across provider 429/503 responses.
Treat 429 as a failed charge and create a new payment intent when the customer retries.
Call the provider first, then reject with 429 if the tenant has exceeded its local budget.
Apply one global attempt cap without tenant scope, allowing a single tenant to consume the shared limit.
Ignore Retry-After and retry 429/503 immediately using a new provider key.

prompt: A tenant’s payment attempts are capped per minute. Provider responses may time out or return 429/503, and the customer must not be charged twice. What quota response and retry rule should the API use?

feedback.reason: Durable acceptance protects high-risk cases, while priority bands and fair service distribute scarce processing across classes. Lower-value overload needs an explicit response.
feedback.details: Persist high-risk case identity before ACK. Use bounded capacity, reserve admission for high-risk work, and schedule bands with a fairness rule that prevents indefinite routine starvation. When low-value capacity is full, return defer/reject rather than silently dropping accepted work. Keep acceptance durability distinct from later analyst throughput.

messages.text: A routine backlog can block high-risk cases that the policy must protect.
Strict priority can starve the lower band indefinitely instead of providing fairness.
Accepted cases must be durable; later silent shedding makes the acknowledgment false.
Priority cannot recover a case lost when the process restarts.

options.text: Reserve durable admission for high-risk cases; defer routine work with explicit backpressure.
Use one FIFO queue for all cases and allow routine traffic to occupy every admission slot.
Always process high-risk cases first and never service routine cases while any high-risk case exists.
Acknowledge all submissions and discard lower-priority cases later if storage fills.
Place high-risk cases at the front of an in-memory queue and return accepted before persistence.

prompt: Fraud review capacity is limited. High-risk cases must persist after acceptance; routine low-value cases may be deferred or rejected. Analysts need fair priority bands rather than one class starving forever. What overload policy meets this?

feedback.reason: Export cost is bounded per tenant and period, while stable identity pins the historical output. Admission precedes expensive compute and acceptance records the snapshot.
feedback.details: Estimate/budget export cost and enforce per-tenant/per-period limits before computation. Schedule fairly across tenants. Persist a durable exportId with the period, source cutoff, and rules revision before acknowledging acceptance. If capacity is unavailable, defer/reject visibly. A retry retrieves the pinned artifact; it does not recalculate latest data.

messages.text: A global quota lacks tenant fairness and lets one tenant monopolize expensive export capacity.
The same exportId would then return different bytes and lose historical reproducibility.
Durability alone does not bound costly demand or make queued work running.
The expensive work has already consumed capacity before admission enforcement.

options.text: Limit exports per tenant and period; pin every accepted job to one immutable snapshot.
Use a single global export quota so a high-volume tenant can consume all available job slots.
When a tenant retries under load, recalculate the export from the latest payroll snapshot to save stored artifact space.
Accept unlimited exports into a durable queue and report them as running before a worker starts.
Calculate the full export first, then reject the tenant if its CPU budget was exceeded.

prompt: Payroll export jobs consume significant CPU. Each tenant may request only a bounded number per period, and accepted exports must remain reproducible under their exportId. What quota contract fits?

feedback.reason: Tenant budgets control cost, and a single snapshot cutoff preserves report meaning. Overload must be explicit or clearly labeled stale.
feedback.details: Check tenant cost/concurrency budget before running the query. If accepted, bind all reads to one consistent snapshot and return the cutoff. If capacity is unavailable, reject/defer or return cached data with explicit as-of freshness; never mix partial results from different snapshots. Fairness and consistency both need visible contracts.

messages.text: Different source cutoffs can produce a total that never existed at one point in time.
The required fairness is per tenant; global accounting leaves noisy-neighbor behavior.
The caller cannot determine whether the report meets the consistency/freshness requirement.
Late enforcement cannot protect query resources.

options.text: Apply a per-tenant cost budget and a consistent cutoff; reject overload before partial totals.
Read whichever table results are available and combine them under one report total when a query exceeds budget.
Use one global budget and let a large tenant consume all query slots.
Return cached results during overload without indicating their cutoff or age.
Run the expensive report and only afterward decide whether the tenant had enough remaining budget.

prompt: Financial report queries have a cost limit per tenant. The report must use one consistent cutoff, and overload may return reject or an explicitly stale result—but must not silently combine snapshots. Which policy is correct?
